summary: A University of Michigan review of 281 studies from 36 countries, published in BMJ, found that about 14% of adults and 12% of children show signs of addiction to ultra-processed foods, levels close to those for alcohol and tobacco. Researchers say fast delivery of fats and carbs and flavor and texture additives may make these foods addictive. Two outside dietitians offered cautions: one lists warning signs and urges more minimally processed foods, while the other doubts food is addictive like drugs. All agreed more research is needed.
one_line: A University of Michigan review in BMJ finds roughly 14% of adults and 12% of children show addiction-like signs toward ultra-processed foods, though outside experts urge caution.
key_facts: The University of Michigan researchers reviewed 281 studies from 36 different countries.
The review found 14% of adults and 12% of children showed signs of addiction to ultra-processed foods, measured by the Yale Food Addiction Scale (YFAS).
These rates are close to the addiction levels seen for alcohol and tobacco, according to the study article published in the journal BMJ.
Ultra-processed foods are high in carbohydrates and fats, such as candy, ice cream and potato chips.

Researchers wrote that ultra-processed foods deliver fats and carbs to the gut much faster than minimally processed foods, and contain flavor and texture additives that could make them more addictive.

Lead researcher Ashley Gearhardt, a University of Michigan psychology professor, said there is "converging and consistent support for the validity and clinical relevance of ultra-processed food addiction."
Gearhardt noted that 103 countries have passed sugar-sweetened beverage taxes, and more than 20 countries have added nutrition labels to these foods.

Dietitian Tanya Freirich listed warning signs of food addiction, including obsessive thoughts about food, craving food when not hungry, eating past fullness, reduced control over intake, withdrawal symptoms, and continuing to eat despite negative consequences.
Dietitian Erin Palinski-Wade is skeptical that food is as addictive as drugs, saying sugar is not addictive the way cocaine is and that reducing it will not cause true withdrawal.
Palinski-Wade said foods high in added sugar or fat trigger dopamine release, and eating more builds dopamine tolerance, requiring more food for the same pleasure response.

Freirich pointed out the study was a review compiling data from other studies, and suggested a controlled trial comparing ultra-processed and minimally processed meal plans while measuring cravings and dopamine levels.

Freirich recommended filling most meals with minimally processed foods, and Palinski-Wade advised those with binge-eating or uncontrolled cravings to work with a therapist or registered dietitian experienced in eating disorders.
The experts all agreed more research is needed to understand the relationship between food and addiction.
